messages.subject: Re: Removing NA from stacked distribution bargraphs
parts:
I would suggest that the missing data is informative and your graph is better as is since there is an increasing trend in missing responses over time, but if you really want yearly sums of 1, I'd suggest removing the NAs in the data before passing it to ggplot(); e.g.,

ds1 <- subset(ds, !is.na(attend))
ggplot(ds1, ...) + ...

or

ggplot(subset(ds, !is.na(attend)), ...) + ...


BTW, as an exercise, try this in the R console:

ds <- read.table(header = TRUE, text = "
<copy/paste the data from your message here>
")

and see what happens. This is why copy/paste from the console is not helpful to those who are trying to help you. See ?dput and Google "R reproducible example" for better ways to send data via e-mail to text-oriented mailing lists.

Dennis 




On Sat, Jun 21, 2014 at 11:45 AM, Andrey K. <koval....@gmail.com> wrote:

Data description:

dsL<-readRDS("./Data/Derived/dsL.rds")
# color palette for the outcome
attcol8<-c("Never"="#4575b4",
           "Once or Twice"="#74add1",
           "Less than once/month"="#abd9e9",
           "About once/month"="#e0f3f8",
           "About twice/month"="#fee090",
           "About once/week"="#fdae61",
           "Several times/week"="#f46d43",
           "Everyday"="#d73027")

# view for one respondent
print (dsL[dsL$id==1,c("id","year","attend","attendF")])

   id year attend         attendF
1   1 1997     NA            <NA>
2   1 1998     NA            <NA>
3   1 1999     NA            <NA>
4   1 2000      1           Never
5   1 2001      6 About once/week
6   1 2002      2   Once or Twice
7   1 2003      1           Never
8   1 2004      1           Never
9   1 2005      1           Never
10  1 2006      1           Never
11  1 2007      1           Never
12  1 2008      1           Never
13  1 2009      1           Never
14  1 2010      1           Never
15  1 2011      1           Never

Creating frequency distributions for each of the measurement wave we have:

ds<- dsL
p<-ggplot(ds, aes(x=yearF, fill=attendF))
p<-p+ geom_bar(position="fill")
p<-p+ scale_fill_manual(values = attcol8,
                    name="Response category" )
p<-p+ scale_y_continuous("Prevalence: proportion of total",
                     limits=c(0, 1),
                     breaks=c(.1,.2,.3,.4,.5,.6,.7,.8,.9,1))
p<-p+ scale_x_discrete("Waves of measurement",
                   limits=as.character(c(2000:2011)))
p<-p+ labs(title=paste0("In the past year, how often have you attended a worship service?"))
p

Missing values are used in the calculation of total responses to show the natural attrition in the study. Assuming that attrition is not significantly associated with the outcome measure, we can remove missing values from the calculation of the total of responses and at look at percentages that each response was endorsed at each time point.

The question is, what can be done to reproduce the graph above without the missing values used in the calcualtion of the total?  I tried na.rm=TRUE in various places, but it didn't go the trick. Ideally, i'd prefer the solution that disturbs the ggplot the least. Any ideas?

ds<- dsL
### ???
p<-ggplot(ds, aes(x=yearF, fill=attendF))
p<-p+ geom_bar(position="fill")
p<-p+ scale_fill_manual(values = attcol8,
                    name="Response category" )
p<-p+ scale_y_continuous("Prevalence: proportion of total",
                     limits=c(0, 1),
                     breaks=c(.1,.2,.3,.4,.5,.6,.7,.8,.9,1))
p<-p+ scale_x_discrete("Waves of measurement",
                   limits=as.character(c(2000:2011)))
p<-p+ labs(title=paste0("In the past year, how often have you attended a worship service?"))
#p
